questions.question: A service receives 1,000 requests per second and each request spends 80 ms in the system. Approximately how many requests must be in flight before adding safety headroom?
questions.explanation: Little's Law gives average in-flight work as arrival rate multiplied by time in the system: 1,000 × 0.08 seconds = 80.

questions.question: Why is starting one goroutine for every incoming request not a complete overload-control strategy?
options: Goroutines cannot perform network I/O
Goroutines always use one operating-system thread each
The runtime can schedule many goroutines, but downstream capacity, memory, queues, and useful work still require explicit bounds
A goroutine cannot be cancelled
questions.explanation: Cheap scheduling does not create downstream or CPU capacity. Admission and worker bounds keep overload visible and contain queueing.

questions.question: For a CPU-bound workload on an eight-core host, what usually happens when worker count grows far beyond the available CPU parallelism?
options: Useful throughput grows linearly forever
Scheduling and queueing increase while useful throughput approaches the CPU limit
Every goroutine receives a dedicated core
The Go runtime automatically rejects new goroutines
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work is limited by available execution capacity. Extra runnable goroutines mostly wait and add scheduling pressure.

questions.question: Who should close a jobs channel with several workers receiving from it?
options: The sender that owns completion of all sends
The first worker that receives a job
Every worker when it finishes
The garbage collector
questions.explanation: The sending side that knows no more values will be produced owns closure. Multiple receivers cannot safely infer global send completion.

questions.question: A producer can block on jobs <- job after the request context is cancelled. What is the safer send pattern?
options: Increase the channel buffer until blocking becomes impossible
Start another detached goroutine to perform the send
Use select with both the send case and ctx.Done()
Close the channel from the producer on every timeout
questions.explanation: Selecting on the send and cancellation lets admission stop when the work is no longer useful instead of leaking a blocked producer.

questions.question: What does a buffered channel primarily provide?
options: Permanent storage for jobs
A bounded decoupling window between producers and consumers
Guaranteed higher throughput for every workload
Automatic retry and deduplication
questions.explanation: A buffer absorbs a bounded mismatch in timing. It does not replace durable storage, overload policy, or capacity.

questions.question: Why should the same context reach admission, workers, and downstream calls?
options: It guarantees every operation completes successfully
It makes channels unnecessary
It lets cancellation and deadlines stop work across the full ownership path
It increases GOMAXPROCS
questions.explanation: End-to-end propagation keeps queued, active, and downstream work tied to the caller or service lifecycle that owns it.

questions.question: Which production check is best at exposing accidental shared-memory races in Go tests?
options: go test -race
go fmt
go env
go doc
questions.explanation: The race detector instruments memory access and reports conflicting unsynchronized reads and writes exercised by the test workload.
